This report contains a formal specification of the Uniswap exchange model (constant product market maker model) that includes a description of price discovery including fees, tokens trading and adding/removing liquidity.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eSince the implementation is restricted to integer arithmetic, the main purpose of the RV report is to analyze the difference between the theoretical model and the implemented model. This report only analyzes rounding errors that are made on the transition to integer arithmetics. It proves that no attack can be made to benefit from rounding errors, and that every rounding error is made in favour of the liquidity pool.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe RV report does the disadvantage of being a newer language with a smaller community, thus having fewer security analysis tools available. Fortunately, Vyper's design philosophy priortizes both auditability and legibility. The LLL IR from the compiler made it easier to see which opcodes are used to achieve the written instructions.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eDespite Vyper's emphasis on legibility, we observed some unituitive output from the compiler. In particular, the built in function \u003ccode\u003ecreate_with_code_of(address)\u003c/code\u003e does not use the code of the input address, but rather creates a contract which delegates it's logic to the input address.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eOn the quality and preparedness of Uniswap\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-on-the-quality-and-preparedness-of-uniswap\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: On the quality and preparedness of Uniswap\" href=\"#on-the-quality-and-preparedness-of-uniswap\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eUniswap's documentation is thorough and well written. The codebase contains natspec comments on each function. The code is written defensively, with frequent assert statements to revert calls with invalid input.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eWe found the test coverage to be incomplete. Including untested behavior, and sections of code which were untested. The majority of the tests are positive test cases, meaning that the tests confirm that the system works with an expected sequence of actions and inputs. The test suite should be expanded to include more negative scenarios to ensure that the safe checks within the contract system are working correctly.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e1.5 Recommendations\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-15-recommendations\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: 1.5 Recommendations\" href=\"#15-recommendations\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe issues in our report do not necesessitate replacing the system as it currently stands.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eAn important consideration in our recommendation is that the Uniswap system has been live on the main Ethereum network for several months, and holds over $300,000 in its liquidity pools. This provides a natural incentive to attack the system, suggesting that no known vulnerabilities currently exist.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eOur primary recommendation is to extend the test suite to cover 100% of the code, and to include testing to ensure for undesirable behavior.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 tabindex=\"-1\" The functionality in these contracts is fairly minimal, and the implementation in vyper has likely mitigated many of the classic implementation errors, so it seems like an attacker is going to have the most luck attacking extra features in the attached ERC20 token.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eMalicious Trader\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-malicious-trader\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Malicious Trader\" href=\"#malicious-trader\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eTwo key areas of attack for malicious traders would be trying to stack rounding issues, and skimming trades via front running. Rounding issues are unlikely to be much of a problem because rounding always favors the liquidity providers, but is likely to be a key attack vector for a while. Specifics and potential mitigations are discussed in \u003cstrong\u003e3.1\u003c/strong\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eMalicious Miner\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-malicious-miner\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Malicious Miner\" href=\"#malicious-miner\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe key advantage that a Malicious Miner has is the ability to front run transactions much more reliably. Hopefully the social incentives for being a fair pool operator will preclude any of the major pools from participating in this sort of activity, but the threat exists.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eMalicious Liquidity Provider\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-malicious-liquidity-provider\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Malicious Liquidity Provider\" href=\"#malicious-liquidity-provider\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eA large liquidity provider primarily has the advantage when performing rounding attacks. Since rounding errors favor the liquidity provider, someone may temporarily take something like a 95% stake in the liquidity pool, and then attempt to stack rounding issues to drain funds from the liquidity pool. We have so far been unable to figure out a sequence of events that would be favorable to the attacker.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eMalicious Exchange Creator\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-malicious-exchange-creator\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Malicious Exchange Creator\" href=\"#malicious-exchange-creator\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eImportantly, anyone can create an exchange, and can set it to any ERC20 token they like, which could lead to a few types of attacks. An attacker may attempt to impersonate a popular token by naming it similarly, though as long as the default exchanges are statically added to the frontend manually exposure should be limited.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eMore interestingly, the exchange creator could register a well known legitimate token, but initialize the liquidity pool in such a way that the token can never be used on the platform.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThere is also nothing in Uniswap to ensure a token address provided to the the Factory, is compliant with ERC20. However, Exchange contracts are created via a template, so the Exchange code can't be tampered with. The ERC20 tokens could be contracts designed to attack Uniswap, or particularly vulnerable contracts might be added more prone to attack.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch4 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003eMalicious Web Attacker\u003c/h4\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-malicious-web-attacker\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: Malicious Web Attacker\" href=\"#malicious-web-attacker\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eSince the front-facing portion of Uniswap is hosted on a website, anyone who gains access to the DNS, hosting, or Cloudflare account could deploy a malicious Uniswap frontend that could, among other things, redirect transactions meant for the Exchanges to a wallet controlled by the attacker. An attacker may also go after one of the many dependencies pulled in by NPM to inject themselves into the deployment process.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch2 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e3 Issue Overview\u003c/h2\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-3-issue-overview\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: 3 Issue Overview\" href=\"#3-issue-overview\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe following table contains all the issues discovered during the audit. dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eDescription\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIf token allows making reentrancy on \u003ccode\u003etransferFrom(address from, address to, uint tokens)\u003c/code\u003e function by someone except the recipient, then all the liquidity funds might be stolen. For example, if token calls callback function of \u003ccode\u003efrom\u003c/code\u003e address. It's irrelevant if reentrancy is done before or after the balances update.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAttack\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eLet's imagine we have a token that calls a callback function of \u003ccode\u003efrom\u003c/code\u003e address on \u003ccode\u003etransferFrom(address from, address to, uint tokens)\u003c/code\u003e and allows \u003ccode\u003efrom\u003c/code\u003e address to make a reentrancy.  We will consider the case when reentrancy is made after the token balances are updated. If token balances are updated after the reentrancy (e.g. ERC-777), the algorithm is even easier and requires fewer funds to steal liquidity pool.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eIn \u003ccode\u003etokenToTokenInput \u003c/code\u003e we have the following 2 lines of code\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto\" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content=\"assert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)\ntokens_bought: uint256 = Exchange(exchange_addr).ethToTokenTransferInput(min_tokens_bought, deadline, recipient, value=wei_bought)\"\u003e\u003cpre class=\"notranslate\"\u003e\u003ccode\u003eassert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)\ntokens_bought: uint256 = Exchange(exchange_addr).ethToTokenTransferInput(min_tokens_bought, deadline, recipient, value=wei_bought)\n\u003c/code\u003e\u003c/pre\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eAttacker(\u003ccode\u003ebuyer\u003c/code\u003e) can make reentrancy on the first line here.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col dir=\"auto\"\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAssume we have an exchange with a token that worth equally to ETH with liquidity pool equals (100 tokens, 100 ETH)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAn attacker creates a fake Exchange (it will be the second exchange in \u003ccode\u003etokenToToken\u003c/code\u003e transfers) that will receive ETH from the first exchange and behave like a normal exchange.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe attacker can buy 50 ETH for 100 tokens by using \u003ccode\u003etokenToTokenInput\u003c/code\u003e function.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNew liquidity pool should be (200 tokens, 50 ETH) but since the attacker makes reentrancy on \u003ccode\u003eassert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)\u003c/code\u003e it will still be (200 tokens, 100 ETH).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eWhile making reentrancy the attacker can buy 49.999 ETH for about 200 tokens using \u003ccode\u003etokenToEthSwapInput\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAfter that, the liquidity pool should look like (400 tokens, 0.001 ETH)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eNow the attacker can buy all the tokens for a very small amount of ETH.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThis is not a very accurate algorithm that does not include fees and gas cost, but logic stays the same.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eRemediation\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eAdd mutex to all functions that make trades in order to prevent reentrancy.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" height: auto; max-height: 30px;\"\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca href=\"https://github.com/ConsenSys/Uniswap-audit-internal-2018-12/issues/30\"\u003e issues/30\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003eThe issue is currently under review\u003c/td\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/tbody\u003e\n\u003c/table\u003e\u003c/markdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThe default client contains a constant called \u003ccode\u003eALLOWED_SLIPPAGE\u003c/code\u003e which states how much the price is allowed to change. This constant is set to 0.025 in \u003ccode\u003euniswap-frontend/src/pages/Swap/index.js:367\u003c/code\u003e. This means that the price can go up ~2.5% from what the buyer expects, and the order will still get executed.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eAny user on the Ethereum network has the ability to watch for new transactions being sent to the network. When the attacker sees a large victim transaction that they want to front run come in, they can create a similar transaction that would move the market up by no more than 2.5%. They then increase their gas fees to ensure that their order gets executed first. The attacker transaction executes, raising the price of the asset, and then the victim transaction executes at the higher price. The attacker is then free to exit the position immediately, pocketing the difference, having never exposed themselves to any risk.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eSophisicated front-runners will likely call these transactions from their own contract addresses to make sure they end up with the prices they expect, and don't collide with other front-runners.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eThis is a hard problem in general, and front-running of some form is always to be expected. By reducing the \u003ccode\u003eALLOWED_SLIPPAGE\u003c/code\u003e (maybe even to 0), you can reduce the amount that front-runners can get for free from every transaction. The slippage value should probabally also be exposed to the user so they can opt in to a 0% slippage value if they choose.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eEven with zero slippage, the attacker can still make a large buy order, watch the victims order fail, wait until they make a new order, and then exit their position. Doing this does carry the additional risk that the victim may be unhappy with the new price, which eliminates the attackers opportunity for zero risk skimming.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp dir=\"auto\"\u003eBancor uses a front-running mitigation where there was a maximum gas value, so a user using the maximum gas value cannot be front-run by an attacker increasing the gas for their transaction. This approach might be worth looking into.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv class=\"markdown-heading\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e\u003ch3 tabindex=\"-1\" class=\"heading-element\" dir=\"auto\"\u003e3.3 Gaps in test coverage (\u003ca href=\"https://github.com/ConsenSys/Uniswap-audit-internal-2018-12/issues/32\"\u003e#32\u003c/a\u003e)\u003c/h3\u003e\u003ca id=\"user-content-33-gaps-in-test-coverage-32\" class=\"anchor\" aria-label=\"Permalink: 3.3 Gaps in test coverage (#32)\" href=\"#33-gaps-in-test-coverage-32\"\u003e\u003csvg data-component=\"Octicon\" class=\"octicon octicon-link\" viewBox=\"0 0 16 16\" version=\"1.1\" width=\"16\" height=\"16\" aria-hidden=\"true\"\u003e\u003cpath d=\"m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z\"\u003e\u003c/path\u003e\u003c/svg\u003e\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cmarkdown-accessiblity-table\u003e\u003ctable\u003e\n\u003cthead\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eSeverity\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eStatus\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eLink\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003cth\u003eRemediation Comment\u003c/th\u003e\n\u003c/tr\u003e\n\u003c/thead\u003e\n\u003ctbody\u003e\n\u003ctr\u003e\n\u003ctd\u003e\u003ca target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener noreferrer\" href=\"/ConsenSysDiligence/Uniswap-audit-report-2018-12/blob/master/static-content/minor.png\"\u003e\u003cimg height=\"30px\" src=\"/ConsenSysDiligence/Uniswap-audit-report-2018-12/raw/master/static-content/minor.png\" style=\"max-width: 100%; <div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">1 Summary</h2><a id="user-content-1-summary" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 1 Summary" href="#1-summary"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Uniswap is a decentralized exchange hosted on the main Ethereum blockchain. It enables users to trade any ERC20 token for ETH, or for another ERC20 token. It has no native token, and no fees are charged by Uniswap's creators. Thus it can be considered a public good.</p>
<p dir="auto">From December 10 to January 11 (excluding holidays) four members of the ConsenSys Diligence team conducted a security audit on the Uniswap system.</p>
<p dir="auto">Unsiwap is written in <a href="http://vyper.readthedocs.io" rel="nofollow">Vyper</a>, whereas the vast majority of contracts have been written in Solidity. To our knowledge, this is the first security audit conducted on a Vyper codebase.</p>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">1.2 Audit Goals</h3><a id="user-content-12-audit-goals" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 1.2 Audit Goals" href="#12-audit-goals"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The focus of the audit was to verify that the smart contract system is secure, resilient and working according to its specifications. The audit activities can be grouped in the following three categories:</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Security:</strong> Identifying security related issues within each contract and within the system of contracts.
<strong>Sound Architecture:</strong> Evaluation of the architecture of this system through the lens of established smart contract best practices and general software best practices.
<strong>Code Correctness and Quality:</strong> A full review of the contract source code. The primary areas of focus include:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Correctness</li>
<li>Readability</li>
<li>Sections of code with high complexity</li>
<li>Quantity and quality of test coverage</li>
</ul>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Summary of Formal Verification work done by Runtime Verification</h4><a id="user-content-summary-of-formal-verification-work-done-by-runtime-verification" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Summary of Formal Verification work done by Runtime Verification" href="#summary-of-formal-verification-work-done-by-runtime-verification"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">We were provided with a <a href="https://github.com/runtimeverification/verified-smart-contracts/blob/uniswap/uniswap/x-y-k.pdf">report</a> by Runtime Verification (RV) Inc. describing some properties of Uniswap exchange. This report contains a formal specification of the Uniswap exchange model (constant product market maker model) that includes a description of price discovery including fees, tokens trading and adding/removing liquidity.</p>
<p dir="auto">Since the implementation is restricted to integer arithmetic, the main purpose of the RV report is to analyze the difference between the theoretical model and the implemented model. This report only analyzes rounding errors that are made on the transition to integer arithmetics. It proves that no attack can be made to benefit from rounding errors, and that every rounding error is made in favour of the liquidity pool.</p>
<p dir="auto">The RV report does not cover all possible attacks on the actual smart contract system, such as frontrunning, reentrancy, etc.</p>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">On Auditing Vyper</h4><a id="user-content-on-auditing-vyper" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: On Auditing Vyper" href="#on-auditing-vyper"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Vyper has the disadvantage of being a newer language with a smaller community, thus having fewer security analysis tools available. Fortunately, Vyper's design philosophy priortizes both auditability and legibility. The LLL IR from the compiler made it easier to see which opcodes are used to achieve the written instructions.</p>
<p dir="auto">Despite Vyper's emphasis on legibility, we observed some unituitive output from the compiler. In particular, the built in function <code>create_with_code_of(address)</code> does not use the code of the input address, but rather creates a contract which delegates it's logic to the input address.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">On the quality and preparedness of Uniswap</h4><a id="user-content-on-the-quality-and-preparedness-of-uniswap" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: On the quality and preparedness of Uniswap" href="#on-the-quality-and-preparedness-of-uniswap"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Uniswap's documentation is thorough and well written. The codebase contains natspec comments on each function. The code is written defensively, with frequent assert statements to revert calls with invalid input.</p>
<p dir="auto">We found the test coverage to be incomplete. Including untested behavior, and sections of code which were untested. The majority of the tests are positive test cases, meaning that the tests confirm that the system works with an expected sequence of actions and inputs. The test suite should be expanded to include more negative scenarios to ensure that the safe checks within the contract system are working correctly.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">1.5 Recommendations</h3><a id="user-content-15-recommendations" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 1.5 Recommendations" href="#15-recommendations"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The issues in our report do not necesessitate replacing the system as it currently stands.</p>
<p dir="auto">An important consideration in our recommendation is that the Uniswap system has been live on the main Ethereum network for several months, and holds over $300,000 in its liquidity pools. This provides a natural incentive to attack the system, suggesting that no known vulnerabilities currently exist.</p>
<p dir="auto">Our primary recommendation is to extend the test suite to cover 100% of the code, and to include testing to ensure for undesirable behavior.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h2 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">2 Threat Model</h2><a id="user-content-2-threat-model" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2 Threat Model" href="#2-threat-model"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">2.1 Overview</h3><a id="user-content-21-overview" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2.1 Overview" href="#21-overview"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Uniswap is a decentralized exchange, which, from the start, gives it a large number of potential adversaries with strong incentives to take advantage of the system. Here we examine the various malicious actors, and the potential impact they may have on the system.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">2.2 Detail</h3><a id="user-content-22-detail" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 2.2 Detail" href="#22-detail"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Ethereum Attacker</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-ethereum-attacker" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Ethereum Attacker" href="#malicious-ethereum-attacker"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The contracts are live on mainnet, giving anyone the ability to poke at them. The functionality in these contracts is fairly minimal, and the implementation in vyper has likely mitigated many of the classic implementation errors, so it seems like an attacker is going to have the most luck attacking extra features in the attached ERC20 token.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Trader</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-trader" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Trader" href="#malicious-trader"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Two key areas of attack for malicious traders would be trying to stack rounding issues, and skimming trades via front running. Rounding issues are unlikely to be much of a problem because rounding always favors the liquidity providers, but is likely to be a key attack vector for a while. Specifics and potential mitigations are discussed in <strong>3.1</strong>.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Miner</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-miner" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Miner" href="#malicious-miner"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">The key advantage that a Malicious Miner has is the ability to front run transactions much more reliably. Hopefully the social incentives for being a fair pool operator will preclude any of the major pools from participating in this sort of activity, but the threat exists.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Liquidity Provider</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-liquidity-provider" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Liquidity Provider" href="#malicious-liquidity-provider"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">A large liquidity provider primarily has the advantage when performing rounding attacks. Since rounding errors favor the liquidity provider, someone may temporarily take something like a 95% stake in the liquidity pool, and then attempt to stack rounding issues to drain funds from the liquidity pool. We have so far been unable to figure out a sequence of events that would be favorable to the attacker.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Exchange Creator</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-exchange-creator" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Exchange Creator" href="#malicious-exchange-creator"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Importantly, anyone can create an exchange, and can set it to any ERC20 token they like, which could lead to a few types of attacks. An attacker may attempt to impersonate a popular token by naming it similarly, though as long as the default exchanges are statically added to the frontend manually exposure should be limited.</p>
<p dir="auto">More interestingly, the exchange creator could register a well known legitimate token, but initialize the liquidity pool in such a way that the token can never be used on the platform.</p>
<p dir="auto">There is also nothing in Uniswap to ensure a token address provided to the the Factory, is compliant with ERC20. However, Exchange contracts are created via a template, so the Exchange code can't be tampered with. The ERC20 tokens could be contracts designed to attack Uniswap, or particularly vulnerable contracts might be added more prone to attack.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h4 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">Malicious Web Attacker</h4><a id="user-content-malicious-web-attacker" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: Malicious Web Attacker" href="#malicious-web-attacker"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>
<p dir="auto">Since the front-facing portion of Uniswap is hosted on a website, anyone who gains access to the DNS, hosting, or Cloudflare account could deploy a malicious Uniswap frontend that could, among other things, redirect transactions meant for the Exchanges to a wallet controlled by the attacker. An attacker may also go after one of the many dependencies pulled in by NPM to inject themselves into the deployment process.</p>

<p dir="auto"><strong>Description</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">If token allows making reentrancy on <code>transferFrom(address from, address to, uint tokens)</code> function by someone except the recipient, then all the liquidity funds might be stolen. For example, if token calls callback function of <code>from</code> address. It's irrelevant if reentrancy is done before or after the balances update.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Attack</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Let's imagine we have a token that calls a callback function of <code>from</code> address on <code>transferFrom(address from, address to, uint tokens)</code> and allows <code>from</code> address to make a reentrancy.  We will consider the case when reentrancy is made after the token balances are updated. If token balances are updated after the reentrancy (e.g. ERC-777), the algorithm is even easier and requires fewer funds to steal liquidity pool.</p>
<p dir="auto">In <code>tokenToTokenInput </code> we have the following 2 lines of code</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="assert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)
tokens_bought: uint256 = Exchange(exchange_addr).ethToTokenTransferInput(min_tokens_bought, deadline, recipient, value=wei_bought)"><pre class="notranslate"><code>assert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)
tokens_bought: uint256 = Exchange(exchange_addr).ethToTokenTransferInput(min_tokens_bought, deadline, recipient, value=wei_bought)
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">Attacker(<code>buyer</code>) can make reentrancy on the first line here.</p>
<ol dir="auto">
<li>Assume we have an exchange with a token that worth equally to ETH with liquidity pool equals (100 tokens, 100 ETH)</li>
<li>An attacker creates a fake Exchange (it will be the second exchange in <code>tokenToToken</code> transfers) that will receive ETH from the first exchange and behave like a normal exchange.</li>
<li>The attacker can buy 50 ETH for 100 tokens by using <code>tokenToTokenInput</code> function.</li>
<li>New liquidity pool should be (200 tokens, 50 ETH) but since the attacker makes reentrancy on <code>assert self.token.transferFrom(buyer, self, tokens_sold)</code> it will still be (200 tokens, 100 ETH).</li>
<li>While making reentrancy the attacker can buy 49.999 ETH for about 200 tokens using <code>tokenToEthSwapInput</code>.</li>
<li>After that, the liquidity pool should look like (400 tokens, 0.001 ETH)</li>
<li>Now the attacker can buy all the tokens for a very small amount of ETH.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">This is not a very accurate algorithm that does not include fees and gas cost, but logic stays the same.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Remediation</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Add mutex to all functions that make trades in order to prevent reentrancy.</p>

(<a href="https://github.com/ConsenSys/Uniswap-audit-internal-2018-12/issues/30">#30</a>)</h3><a id="user-content-32-frontrunners-can-skim-25-from-every-transaction-30" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.2 Frontrunners can skim ~2.5% from every transaction. <p dir="auto">The default client contains a constant called <code>ALLOWED_SLIPPAGE</code> which states how much the price is allowed to change. This constant is set to 0.025 in <code>uniswap-frontend/src/pages/Swap/index.js:367</code>. This means that the price can go up ~2.5% from what the buyer expects, and the order will still get executed.</p>
<p dir="auto">Any user on the Ethereum network has the ability to watch for new transactions being sent to the network. When the attacker sees a large victim transaction that they want to front run come in, they can create a similar transaction that would move the market up by no more than 2.5%. They then increase their gas fees to ensure that their order gets executed first. The attacker transaction executes, raising the price of the asset, and then the victim transaction executes at the higher price. The attacker is then free to exit the position immediately, pocketing the difference, having never exposed themselves to any risk.</p>
<p dir="auto">Sophisicated front-runners will likely call these transactions from their own contract addresses to make sure they end up with the prices they expect, and don't collide with other front-runners.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is a hard problem in general, and front-running of some form is always to be expected. By reducing the <code>ALLOWED_SLIPPAGE</code> (maybe even to 0), you can reduce the amount that front-runners can get for free from every transaction. The slippage value should probabally also be exposed to the user so they can opt in to a 0% slippage value if they choose.</p>
<p dir="auto">Even with zero slippage, the attacker can still make a large buy order, watch the victims order fail, wait until they make a new order, and then exit their position. Doing this does carry the additional risk that the victim may be unhappy with the new price, which eliminates the attackers opportunity for zero risk skimming.</p>
<p dir="auto">Bancor uses a front-running mitigation where there was a maximum gas value, so a user using the maximum gas value cannot be front-run by an attacker increasing the gas for their transaction. This approach might be worth looking into.</p>

<p dir="auto"><strong>Description</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">The test suite could be improved in certain areas. Different types of testing parameters and testing methodologies could be used to further extend its coverage.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Remediation</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Specific areas that were identified as lacking proper coverage:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Additional ERC20 contracts with edge case parameters set (e.g.: <code>decimals = 0 | 18 | MAX_UINT8</code>, <code>totalSupply = 0 | MAX_UINT256</code>, ...) as opposed to only testing with the <code>HAY</code> token</li>
<li>Stress tests with some blackbox fuzzing with random amounts and parameters for ETH <-> ERC20 trades and ERC20 <-> ERC20 trades instead of fixed amounts.</li>
<li>Do unit testing in exchange functions with proper state reset between each test as opposed to doing only end-to-end tests with persisting state.</li>
<li>In the end-to-end tests more scenarios could be added to test for adverse conditions like big slippage.</li>
</ul>

<p dir="auto"><strong>Description</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Many functions in <code>Exchange</code> contract have <code>deadline</code> as a parameter. This parameter has the same description in every function. But some functions use <code>></code> operator when checking for a deadline</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="assert deadline > block.timestamp"><pre class="notranslate"><code>assert deadline > block.timestamp
</code></pre></div>
<p dir="auto">while other functions use <code>>=</code> operator.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Remediation</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Change all <code>></code> operators to <code>>=</code> when working with deadline parameter.
It does not really affect anything but keeps code more beautiful and consistent.</p>

<p dir="auto"><strong>Description</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">In <code>uniswap_factory.vy</code> there are some redundant assertions:</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/Uniswap/contracts-vyper/blob/957f7aba57cec5d87824312dd3dd6484e0220086/contracts/uniswap_factory.vy#L15">contracts/uniswap_factory.vy:L15</a></p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-solidity notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="    assert template != ZERO_ADDRESS"><pre>    <span class="pl-k">assert</span> template <span class="pl-k">!=</span> ZERO_ADDRESS</pre></div>
<p dir="auto">and</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/Uniswap/contracts-vyper/blob/957f7aba57cec5d87824312dd3dd6484e0220086/contracts/uniswap_factory.vy#L21">contracts/uniswap_factory.vy:L21</a></p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-solidity notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="    assert self.exchangeTemplate != ZERO_ADDRESS"><pre>    <span class="pl-k">assert</span> self.exchangeTemplate <span class="pl-k">!=</span> ZERO_ADDRESS</pre></div>
<p dir="auto">Due to the fact that the Vyper compiler actually asserts that the code size at the specified exchange address (through the use of <code>EXTCODESIZE</code>) is bigger than <code>0</code>, here:</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/Uniswap/contracts-vyper/blob/master/contracts/uniswap_factory.vy#L24">contracts/uniswap_factory.vy:L24</a></p>
<div class="highlight highlight-source-solidity notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" dir="auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="    Exchange(exchange).setup(token)"><pre>    <span class="pl-en">Exchange</span>(exchange).<span class="pl-en">setup</span>(token)</pre></div>
<p dir="auto">This meaning that the zeroth address as the exchange, having no code at all, would make the call to <code>setup()</code> fail.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Remediation</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">Remove the two assertions.</p>
<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">3.7 The factory contract should use a constructor (<a href="https://github.com/ConsenSys/Uniswap-audit-internal-2018-12/issues/23">#23</a>)</h3><a id="user-content-37-the-factory-contract-should-use-a-constructor-23" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: 3.7 The factory contract should use a constructor (#23)" href="#37-the-factory-contract-should-use-a-constructor-23"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>

<p dir="auto"><strong>Description</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">The factory uses a public function for initialization instead of a constructor which might make it a target for griefing attacks.</p>
<p dir="auto">Since there is no way to actually deploy the contract and call the <code>initializeFactory()</code> method within the same transaction without an additional contract designed for the effect (which seems to be inexistent in the current codebase) an attacker could grief deployments of the Uniswap factory by always front-running the initializing transaction after deployment.</p>
<p dir="auto">Possibly even more worrisome would be a front-running transaction that would underhandedly change the exchange template code to something very similarly benign but that was, for example, an underhandedly backdoored version of the original.</p>
<p dir="auto"><strong>Remediation</strong></p>
<p dir="auto">The easiest solution would be to turn the initialization method into the constructor of said contract.
Another possible remediation would be to introduce a "factory deployer" contract that executes both message calls in a single transaction.</p>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">A.2.1 - Minor</h3><a id="user-content-a21---minor" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: A.2.1 - Minor" href="#a21---minor"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>

<div class="markdown-heading" dir="auto"><h3 tabindex="-1" class="heading-element" dir="auto">A.2.2 - Medium</h3><a id="user-content-a22---medium" class="anchor" aria-label="Permalink: A.2.2 - Medium" href="#a22---medium"><svg data-component="Octicon" class="octicon octicon-link" viewBox="0 0 16 16" version="1.1" width="16" height="16" aria-hidden="true"><path d="m7.775 3.275 1.25-1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1 4.95 4.95l-2.5 2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1-4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1 .018-1.042.751.751 0 0 1 1.042-.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l2.5-2.5a2.002 2.002 0 0 0-2.83-2.83l-1.25 1.25a.751.751 0 0 1-1.042-.018.751.751 0 0 1-.018-1.042Zm-4.69 9.64a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 2.83 0l1.25-1.25a.751.751 0 0 1 1.042.018.751.751 0 0 1 .018 1.042l-1.25 1.25a3.5 3.5 0 1 1-4.95-4.95l2.5-2.5a3.5 3.5 0 0 1 4.95 0 .751.751 0 0 1-.018 1.042.751.751 0 0 1-1.042.018 1.998 1.998 0 0 0-2.83 0l-2.5 2.5a1.998 1.998 0 0 0 0 2.83Z"></path></svg></a></div>

Key Takeaways: 

- Uniswap’s fee switch links the UNI token to protocol usage through supply burns. Protocol fees now flow into UNI supply reduction, shifting UNI from governance-only to direct value accrual.

- Early data implies ~$26M annualized protocol fees and a ~207x revenue multiple. Ongoing burns of ~4M UNI per year embed high growth expectations into UNI’s $5.4B valuation.

- DeFi is shifting toward fee-linked token models. Burns, staker distributions, and ve-style locking are all attempts to better align tokenholders with protocol economics, shaping how the sector is valued.

@Uniswap 🦄 is the largest Decentralized exchange to date. This is the backstory of @haydenzadams and his journey to founding Uniswap 👇 

Hayden Adams was a mechanical engineer with no formal background in programming or finance.  

His journey into the blockchain space began in 2017 after he was introduced to Ethereum and smart contracts. This was a pivotal moment that steered his career towards creating Uniswap.  

In late 2017, the idea for Uniswap was inspired by a post from Ethereum’s founder @VitalikButerin, discussing automated market makers. Hayden began exploring this concept in depth.  

In 2018, Hayden began learning Solidity, the programming language for Ethereum smart contracts, to develop his business prototype.  

Midway through 2018, he received a grant from the Ethereum Foundation which provided pivotal funding for the early development of Uniswap.  

Uniswap was officially launched in November 2018 and it quickly gained attention for its innovative approach to decentralized trading.  

The year 2020 marked a significant boom in the DeFi space, with Uniswap at the forefront.  

They played a crucial role in popularizing decentralized exchanges, and still continue to grow to this day.  

@moonpay we are proud to be a Uniswap partner, enabling users to purchase crypto using debit card, credit card, or bank transfers directly on the Uniswap platform. 🤝

@haydenzadams'  success story is a testament to the impact of innovative ideas in the blockchain space.  

Salute to Hayden for his work. 🫡

3️⃣ Improvements to Liquidity Infrastructure

Announcing Unichain Developer Grants!

Last week marked the launch of @unichain, a new Ethereum L2 designed for DeFi, and powered by the Superchain.

To drive innovation across Unichain, we’re excited to introduce new grants programs to accelerate the work of DeFi developers.

Unichain Developer Grants will support builders exploring:

1️⃣ Novel Swapping Mechanisms
2️⃣ Innovation upon the DeFi Experience
3️⃣ Improvements to Liquidity Infrastructure

Programs include:

🗣️ Unichain Builder Open Call
Every project has different needs. If you have an idea that can advance our community, apply for opportunities to receive funding, technical support, and go-to-market resources for your project. Apply here: https://t.co/BbwcLQ75qD.

♾️ Unichain Infinite Hackathon
Every hackathon is now a Unichain hackathon. Projects built at competitions around the world can be entered into our Infinite Hackathon, with grants up to $7.5K awarded monthly. Enter here: https://t.co/iE1e8344lZ.

🌀 Unichain Retro Grants
Projects that have demonstrated traction & impact are eligible for up to $7.5K  in grant funding. Submissions will be judged by a dedicated committee of DeFi experts. Nominate a builder here: https://t.co/xjxcGbWmiL.

🧰  Audit Subsidy Fund
Starting in 2025, developers and teams can apply to qualify for funds to cover their audit costs. Program operations will be managed by @areta_io. We're excited to share more details on how to apply for an audit subsidy soon.

🔴 Optimism Collective Grants
As part of the Superchain, Unichain developers can also qualify for @Optimism Collective Grants programs. Learn more about Retro Funding: https://t.co/WiHlgyRLX6 and Governance Fund Grants: https://t.co/DUTw8e3GOA.

⭐️ Get Started
Unichain developers are building the future of DeFi. We’re here to help you begin. Explore our builder toolkit:
https://t.co/HInKfuvt0a

📖  Read More
To learn more about Unichain Developer Grants, dive into the announcement post by Uniswap Foundation's Co-Founder and Head of Growth, @nkennethk: https://t.co/ipbwGS61NX

🤝  Thank you!
Our approach to Unichain Developer Grants has been inspired by the work of Uniswap community developers, and by programs that have successfully contributed to the development of vibrant builder communities, including @Optimism and @eigencloud.
